INTRODUCTION Endometriosis, which is characterized by endometrial implants outside of the endometrial cavity, is a chronic disease that requires a lifelong management plan.
Despite extensive research, the optimal management of endometriosis and its related symptoms is unclear.

The surgical management of pelvic pain due to endometriosis is reviewed here.

GENERAL PRINCIPLES The American Society for Reproductive Medicine Practice Committee states that "endometriosis should be viewed as a chronic disease that requires a lifelong management plan with the goal of maximizing the use of medical treatment and avoiding repeated surgical procedures" [1].

Therefore, treatment decisions are individualized and consider clinical presentation (eg, pain, infertility, mass), symptom severity, disease extent and location, reproductive desires, patient age, medication side effects, surgical complication rates, and cost.
Therapies for endometriosis-related pelvic pain include analgesics, hormonal treatments, and surgical intervention, and a combined approach is often used.
(See "Endometriosis: Treatment of pelvic pain".) Prior to any treatment, all women should have a thorough history and examination, and other causes of pelvic pain should be excluded.

(See "Chronic pelvic pain in adult females: Evaluation".) Surgical intervention provides a histologic diagnosis, allows assessment of pelvic cysts or masses with features concerning for malignancy, and reduces pain by destroying the endometriotic implants [1,2].

Disadvantages of surgery include risk of injury (especially the bowel and bladder), possible reduction of ovarian reserve (eg, after ovarian cyst excision), and adhesion formation, in addition to standard surgical risks.
Deep endometriosis (DIE) is defined as endometriotic nodules penetrating >5 mm below peritoneal surface

drugProtocols: NSAIDs first-line: Ibuprofen 400-800mg PO q6-8h or Naproxen 500mg PO BID
Neuromodulators for central sensitization: Amitriptyline 10-25mg PO qHS, titrate to 75-100mg; OR Gabapentin 100-300mg PO TID, titrate to 900-3600mg/day; OR Duloxetine 30mg PO daily, increase to 60mg

Hormonal suppression: Combined OCP continuous use; OR Norethindrone acetate 5mg PO daily; OR Depot medroxyprogesterone 150mg IM q12 weeks; OR GnRH agonist (Lupron 3.75mg IM monthly) with add-back therapy (Norethindrone 5mg + Estradiol 1mg daily)

If opioids considered: Use lowest effective dose, short-term only, document informed consent, check PDMP, require pain contract

complicationsManagement: If opioid dependence develops: Taper slowly, refer to addiction medicine, switch to buprenorphine if indicated
If depression worsens: Adjust antidepressant, ensure psychiatric follow-up, assess suicidality
If surgical complications from laparoscopy: Manage per standard protocols, document informed consent was obtained

If patient requests hysterectomy as definitive treatment: Counsel that hysterectomy NOT recommended for chronic pelvic pain without identifiable uterine pathology; does not address central sensitization
If pain persists after hysterectomy: Continue multimodal therapy, address persistent central sensitization, pelvic floor dysfunction
If suspected acute intoxication: supportive care, monitor for anxiety/paranoia, benzodiazepines for severe agitation if needed
If drug interaction concern: review CYP450 interactions (cannabis inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2C9)
If cannabis use disorder identified: refer for addiction medicine/psychiatry consultation
If patient reports worsening symptoms with cannabis: discontinue, reassess pain management plan with evidence-based options
If dense adhesions encountered: use sharp dissection, consider preoperative GnRH agonist
If normal ovarian tissue unclear: prioritize ovarian preservation over complete cyst removal
If malignancy suspected intraoperatively: frozen section, avoid cyst rupture, oncology consultation
If recurrence occurs: repeat laparoscopy with cystectomy plus long-term hormonal suppression

decisionPoints: When to consult GI: IBS symptoms unresponsive to treatment, alarm symptoms (weight loss, rectal bleeding, anemia)
When to consult urology: Interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome, hematuria, recurrent UTIs
When to consult pain management: Failed multimodal therapy >6 months, need for interventional procedures, complex medication management
When to refer pelvic floor PT: Pelvic floor muscle tenderness on exam, dyspareunia, levator ani syndrome
When to perform laparoscopy: Suspected endometriosis after failed empiric treatment, adnexal pathology, pelvic adhesions suspected
When to refer psychiatry: PHQ-9 ≥15, active suicidal ideation, substance use disorder, refractory anxiety/depression
When to counsel against use: pregnancy or planning pregnancy, history of substance use disorder, psychiatric conditions, concurrent sedative use
When to suspect cannabis use disorder: using larger amounts than intended, craving, continued use despite problems - 2+ symptoms in 12 months
When to refer: suspected cannabis use disorder, patient requests medical marijuana certification (refer to certifying provider where legal)
Consult gynecologic oncology if: postmenopausal patient, solid components, elevated CA-125
Consider REI referral if: fertility concerns with bilateral endometriomas >3cm
Expectant management appropriate for: asymptomatic cysts <3cm in reproductive-age women
